NE-2025-LB1067.s: The bill changes how the Affordable Housing Trust Fund can be used and managed. It allows transfers from that fund to several other state funds through July 1, 2027, and then stops those transfers after that date. It also changes the rate and split of the documentary stamp tax money that goes into housing funds, including the Rural Workforce Housing Investment Fund and the Middle Income Workforce Housing Investment Fund.

NE-2025-LB1071.s: The bill would set state budget rules and make appropriations for Nebraska state government for FY2025-26 and FY2026-27. It would also carry forward some unspent money, set pay limits for state workers and board members, and let some federal grant money be used above those limits if approved. The visible sections include funding for areas like the Secretary of State, the Department of Revenue’s homestead exemption aid, and several Department of Health and Human Services and Game and Parks programs.

NE-2025-LB1091.s: The bill sets rules for how the Department of Health and Human Services handles long-term care clients with special needs in Medicaid. It would keep skilled nursing and nursing facility care for those clients out of managed care plans, and it would continue that care through fee-for-service Medicaid or another allowed system. It would also bar the department from requiring providers to join a managed care plan just to serve these clients and would require contract changes within six months after the act takes effect.

NE-2025-LB1096.s: The measure was approved by the governor and would add new rules for some consultants working for a Chinese military company in Nebraska. Before they start influencing state policy, they would have to file detailed information and say they are acting for a foreign adversary of the United States. It would also let some public records be kept private and set civil fines of $100,000 per violation, with higher fines for repeat violations.

NE-2025-LB1124.s: The bill would raise the state tax on several tobacco and nicotine products, including snuff, electronic nicotine delivery systems, alternative nicotine products, and other tobacco products. It would also change how the tax is figured and say who must pay it in some sales. The money collected would still be used and split under a state law on cigarette tax proceeds, and the act would become operative on July 1, 2026.

NE-2025-LB1126.s: The bill became law and creates an infrastructure development investment program. It also changes or ends rules tied to rural road districts, local public works contracts, transportation projects, driver safety rules, Medicaid rides for nonemergency medical trips, and wireless phone surcharges. It affects state agencies, local governments, road users, wireless customers, and people who use Medicaid transportation services.

NE-2025-LB1135.s: The measure would update several Nebraska laws on service contracts, parking deals, community development, land banks, and clean energy financing. It would also let certain cities and villages sell waterworks, sewer systems, or water systems to an Indian tribe when the system is within tribal land, the tribe’s headquarters is in that city or village, and local voters approve the sale. The bill was approved by the Governor on April 14, 2026.

NE-2025-LB1195.s: The bill changes rules for female inmates in county jails and requires county and city jails to follow certain standards on cross-gender supervision and searches. It also updates the rules for jail matrons, the staff who help care for women in jail. The bill was approved by the governor.

NE-2025-LB178.s: The bill would require mandatory server alcohol training under Nebraska liquor rules. For special event licenses staffed mostly by volunteers, only the manager on duty would need the training and a state certification. Peace officers would be exempt from the training and certification rules.

NE-2025-LB199.s: The bill would set a two-year time limit for personal injury lawsuits that start on or after its effective date. It would also fold administrative proceedings into Nebraska’s civil litigation funding law and require people using that funding, or their lawyer, to share the funding contract with other parties, the court or agency, and certain insurers or others who may have to pay or defend the claim. It would let the Secretary of State act against a funding company’s registration for certain rule breaks and require yearly reports on funding activity in the state.

NE-2025-LB215.s: The bill would require Nebraska agencies to set up a program for second chance relief for some committed offenders, including people serving long or life sentences. It would let eligible people be reviewed for a sentence commutation, or reduction, after serving 25 years if the offense happened before age 26, or 30 years if it happened at age 26 or older. The process would involve the Department, the Division of Parole Supervision, the Board of Parole, and the Board of Pardons.

NE-2025-LB316.s: The bill would change Nebraska rules for hemp and cannabidiol (CBD) products. It would redefine hemp, set a tax on some CBD products, and change how those products are regulated. It would also change rules for moving hemp and update the state drug law to match these changes.

NE-2025-LB417.s: The bill would put the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska in charge of the Nebraska Promise Program and adopt the College Promise Act. It would also change parts of the Quality Education Accountability Act. Under an amendment, if the federal Pell Grant program is not available in a school year, the board could choose not to run the Nebraska Promise Program for that year and would have to tell students before each year.

NE-2025-LB444.s: The bill would require certain motor carriers in Nebraska to carry at least $1 million in uninsured and underinsured coverage per occupant when insurance rates are set. It would apply to some intrastate carriers, carriers that move household goods, and carriers that transport railroad employees. It would not apply to transportation network companies, which are app-based ride services.

NE-2025-LB455.s: The bill would change Nebraska workers' compensation rules on injury reports and on insurance policies and deductibles. It would also give the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Court a new duty and define one term.

NE-2025-LB468.s: The bill would change several state fee and tax rules. It would set new fees for marriage licenses and vehicle identification inspections, and it would require money from the Securities Act Cash Fund to be sent to the General Fund and the Inheritance Tax Distribution Fund on set dates. It also changes how securities records are handled and fees are paid.

NE-2025-LB522.s: The bill would change when Nebraska workers’ compensation payments start. It would also add yearly cost-of-living adjustments, which are automatic changes to keep benefits in line with rising prices, for weekly income benefits that last more than 12 months. The new adjustment process would begin in 2026 and would affect injured workers receiving these benefits.

NE-2025-LB596.s: The law changes a range of state rules, including legal notices, open meetings, county records, warrants, discharge records, storage for certain records, name-change petitions, marriage license and record fees, abandoned property reports, and the Nebraska Hall of Fame. It also affects the registration of farm, ranch, or home names and removes a penalty for some public officials. The governor approved it on April 14, 2026.

NE-2025-LB646.s: The bill would create an exemption from brand inspections under the Livestock Brand Act and change related fees. A floor amendment would let the brand committee set a surcharge of up to $20 for travel costs tied to each inspection site, to be collected by the brand inspector from the person asking for the inspection or the person required to have it. It also would add a reference to livestock registered under certain state sections.

NE-2025-LB678.s: It would set aside state money for the Board of Trustees of the Nebraska State Colleges for fiscal years 2025-26 and 2026-27. The money would help pay for wage increases in negotiated labor deals, minimum wage changes, and higher health insurance costs.

NE-2025-LB728.s: The bill would require proxy advisors to tell clients and, in some cases, company boards whether their voting advice is based on a written financial analysis. If they do not use that kind of analysis, they would have to say so in the disclosure and on their website. A rule break would count as a deceptive trade practice and could lead to state action or a civil lawsuit by an affected person.

NE-2025-LB784.s: The law changes where some sheriffs may live, what uniforms sheriffs and deputies must wear, and the training sheriffs must complete. It lets some sheriffs run from outside the county, and in some counties they may live in that county or a neighboring one while in office. It also sets uniform rules for sheriffs and deputies and requires yearly continuing education after the first year in office.

NE-2025-LB795.s: This law adds bromazolam to Nebraska’s list of controlled drugs and corrects the spelling of some other drugs in state law. It also raises penalties for some drug crimes involving fentanyl. The law was approved by the governor on March 3, 2026.

NE-2025-LB803.s: Approved by the governor, this law creates a first-time home buyer savings account program and changes several tax and property tax rules in Nebraska. It also changes parts of the sports arena financing law, the property tax growth limit law, homestead exemptions, and income taxes. One added part gives refundable income tax credits to certain groups that serve victims of domestic violence and human trafficking, starting for tax years on or after January 1, 2027.

NE-2025-LB803A.s: The act would set aside state money for the Nebraska Department of Revenue to help carry out Legislative Bill 803. It would give $1,110,157 for FY2026-27 and $986,400 for FY2027-28 for one program, and $177,711 for FY2026-27 and $17,383 for FY2027-28 for another program. It also limits salary and per diem spending in one part and took effect when approved.

NE-2025-LB878.s: It would have given eligible Nebraska state employees paid parental leave after a birth or adoption. Full-time workers would have gotten 240 hours, and part-time workers would have gotten leave based on their regular workweek. The bill said it would start on July 1, 2026, but it failed to become law.

NE-2025-LB894.s: The bill changes rules for the Grain Dealer Act and the Grain Warehouse Act. It would send investment earnings in the Grain Dealer and Grain Warehouse Cash Fund back into that fund, and keep that money from being moved to the General Fund or another state fund. It also states that license fee revenue should not be more than 25% of the commission’s costs to carry out these laws.

NE-2025-LB912.s: This bill became law and changes rules for many health care and child care areas, including training for community health workers, interstate compacts for athletic trainers and respiratory care workers, and several licensing rules. It also changes mental health practice rules by adding required training on domestic abuse for some licensed mental health workers and setting rules for provisional mental health licenses. Some of the added sections are set to take effect on January 1, 2027.

NE-2025-LB937.s: The bill became law and changes several rules for Nebraska schools. It would create the Prior Learning Act and the K-12 Education Cybersecurity Act, and it would also change rules for student transfers, absences, option enrollment, extracurricular activities, school jobs, reports, deadlines, teacher training and hiring programs, and a college pathway program. It would also let absences be excused for a child’s physical or mental illness when a parent or guardian gives documentation from a licensed health professional, with chronic illness papers reviewed each semester.

NE-2025-LB948.s: Nebraska LB 948 changes rules for plant pests, pesticide fees, and the state fertilizer and soil conditioner law. It also ends the Nebraska Poultry and Egg Resources Act, terminates a fund, and removes some rules tied to certain associations and societies. The bill was signed by the governor and became law.

NE-2025-LB958.s: This law changes Medicaid rules to help set up a home and community-based services waiver, give retroactive coverage for some benefits, and pay for doula services, which are trained helpers for people before, during, and after birth. It also changes reporting rules under the Medical Assistance Act, updates the Nebraska Prenatal Plus Program, and sets limits on crisis aid payments under the low-income home energy help program. The doula part says the state must pay for doula services by January 1, 2029, if needed.

NE-2025-LB972A.s: The bill would set funding for several state agencies to carry out LB 972 in fiscal years 2026-27 and 2027-28. It would give money to the Department of Revenue, Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Health and Human Services, Military Department, and Nebraska State Patrol, with amounts ranging from $500 to $1.8 million from different state funds. It was passed by the Legislature and approved by the Governor on April 14, 2026.

NE-2025-LB985.s: Nebraska lawmakers changed rules for guardians and conservators, which are people or companies appointed to help manage someone’s personal or money matters. The changes cover court appointments, removal or resignation, and the powers and duties of guardians and conservators. The bill also gives some people the right to attend certain court hearings and lets courts award costs and expenses in these cases.

NE-2025-LR33.s: This resolution would ask Nebraska’s members of Congress to take action to change how daylight saving time is handled. It says the change should aim to improve health, business output, farm work, public safety, and keep time rules the same across the country. It would also send copies of the resolution to federal leaders and Nebraska’s congressional delegation.

NE-2025-LR372.s: The resolution would direct the Nebraska Retirement Systems Committee to study the state retirement systems overseen by the Public Employees Retirement Board. The study would look at funding needs, benefits, contributions, and how each system is run, and the committee would report its findings and recommendations to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR373.s: The Nebraska Retirement Systems Committee would do an interim study, which is a study done between legislative sessions, on how to carry out a state law about underfunded pension plans. It would focus on defined benefit plans run by local governments and include a public hearing for those governments to give reports. After the study, the committee would send its findings and recommendations to the Legislature.

NE-2025-LR380.s: This resolution would direct a legislative committee to study the needs of youth moving to and from a youth rehabilitation and treatment center, an adult correctional facility, or a residential treatment facility. The study would look at current placement plans, the needs of the youth and their families, other possible facility models, and any law or policy changes needed to carry out a plan based on evidence. The committee would report its findings and recommendations after the study ends.

NE-2025-LR382.s: This resolution would direct an interim study on access to play therapy in Nebraska. The study would look at how well play therapy works, how families get access, billing problems, rules, training and credentials, other states’ approaches, and whether state funding is needed. The Health and Human Services Committee would do the study and report its findings and recommendations.

NE-2025-LR383.s: The resolution would direct the Health and Human Services Committee to study maternal depression in Nebraska and ways state rules or laws could better support maternal mental health. The study would look at data on mothers’ mental health, how it affects babies and families, screening tools, and the help and coverage available for new mothers. It would also review how other states handle the issue and whether more state funding is needed, then report its findings and ideas to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR384.s: The resolution would direct a legislative committee to study the rules for licensing truth and deception examiners in Nebraska. The review would look at whether the current rules best protect the public while also preserving the right to work in a lawful job and supporting more competition and new ideas. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or the Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR385.s: Would direct the Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee to do an interim study of any issues that come up within its area of work. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or the Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR389.s: This resolution would direct the Education Committee to study the school services and learning supports available to deaf and hard of hearing elementary students in Nebraska. The study would look at teacher training, communication supports like sign language interpretation and captioning, early language and reading results, family and school coordination, staff training, and service gaps in rural areas. The committee would also gather input from parents, educators, specialists, educational service units, and state agencies, then report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature.

NE-2025-LR391.s: This resolution would direct the Health and Human Services Committee to study diaper access for Nebraska families. The study would look at how diaper need affects children, mothers, health care, public health, work, and child care, as well as what resources exist in the state and how other states handle it. The committee would then report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR400.s: This resolution would direct the Revenue Committee to do an interim study on state economic development programs, policies, and incentives. The study would make a list of state-run efforts tied to economic growth, jobs, housing, infrastructure, small business, and related tax breaks or federal pass-through funds. It would also look for overlap, gaps, and ways to improve coordination, then report findings and recommendations to the Legislature.

NE-2025-LR403.s: This resolution would direct the Judiciary Committee to study the use of shackling on juveniles. The study would look at when shackling should be barred or allowed, what new rules might be needed, and what other states have done. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR404.s: This legislative resolution would direct the Health and Human Services Committee to do an interim study, which is a review done between sessions. The study would look at Nebraska laws and the rules and tools used for developmental disability waivers and aged and disabled waivers. It would also review waiver eligibility limits, assessment tools, section 1634 Medicaid status, and algorithm-based assessments, then report its findings and recommendations.

NE-2025-LR407.s: Would direct the Urban Affairs Committee to study how culture could help revive Nebraska cities and villages through economic growth, jobs, tourism, and community renewal. The study would also look at possible pilot cultural districts or a statewide cultural title, plus how these ideas might affect underserved communities and different parts of the state. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR415.s: The resolution would direct the Urban Affairs Committee to study how Nebraska law handles labels for real property as blighted and substandard. It would look at current rules, public notice, and how neighborhood associations are involved before a final decision is made. The committee would also gather ideas from other states or cities and report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature.

NE-2025-LR417.s: This resolution would ask the Urban Affairs Committee to study new ways to develop, finance, and own housing in Nebraska. The study would look at tools like tokenized credit systems, community investment models, and digital systems to help with affordable housing and community ownership. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR418.s: The resolution would direct the Urban Affairs Committee to study inland port authorities in Nebraska. The study would look at how these authorities work now and how they are developing land, infrastructure, and local opportunities, then report findings and recommendations to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR419.s: This resolution would call for an interim study, which is a study done between sessions, on volunteer burnout on city boards and commissions. It would also look for specific local boards or commissions that could work with fewer members.

NE-2025-LR423.s: The resolution would direct a legislative study of food insecurity for pregnant and postpartum women and their children in Nebraska. The study would look at the causes, current help like nutrition aid, food banks, and pantries, and how these services affect health and birth outcomes. The Health and Human Services Committee would do the study and report its findings and any recommendations to the Legislature.

NE-2025-LR433.s: The resolution would direct the Legislature’s Education Committee to study how Nebraska can better connect education, training, and jobs for workers in high-demand, high-wage fields. The study would look at data systems, the Nebraska Statewide Workforce and Educational Reporting System, ways to link education and job data, and possible changes to rules on sharing data while protecting privacy. The committee would report its findings and recommendations after the study.

NE-2025-LR434.s: The resolution would direct the Urban Affairs Committee to study how the existing learning community works with and affects the metropolitan class city where it is located. The study would look at rules, funding, student results, special education, and how money is shared among districts and programs. It would also look at work with school districts, cities, and other local groups, and then report findings and recommendations to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR436.s: The resolution would direct the Business and Labor Committee to do an interim study on rules for professional employer organizations. The study would look at the Professional Employer Organization Registration Act and follow state board reform rules. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR441.s: A legislative resolution would direct the Urban Affairs Committee to study how residential and commercial building codes apply and what could happen if LB1227 is enacted. The study would work with the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment to review energy impact studies and look at the return on investment for residential codes. It would also seek a source to explain the return on investment for commercial codes.

NE-2025-LR442.s: A legislative resolution would set up an interim study on youth sports participation in Nebraska. The study would look at equal access, fair play rules, barriers to joining, and the support for fields, centers, and youth groups. The Education Committee would do the study and then report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature.

NE-2025-LR444.s: The resolution would direct the Health and Human Services Committee to study how Nebraska sets payment rates for behavioral health services. The study would look at current rate methods, cost studies, other states’ models, changes in costs since the last state study, and how Medicaid managed care affects rate setting. The committee would then report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR448.s: This resolution would direct a legislative committee to study the quality and availability of help for Nebraska veterans and their families. The study would look at veteran service officers, the benefits they help with, federal rules for their accreditation, related penalties, how veterans learn what benefits they may get, and the veterans disability claims review process. The committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR452.s: The resolution would ask the Appropriations Committee to study how Nebraska funds shared services for youth involved in both child welfare and juvenile justice. The review would look at funding sources, fee and payment rates, oversight, reimbursement, and how costs are shared among state agencies, counties, regions, and providers. It would also look at federal and state money used for these services and compare practices in other states.

NE-2025-LR467.s: The resolution would direct a Nebraska committee to study ways cities, villages, and the state can make Nebraska more appealing to young people, including students, young workers, entrepreneurs, and early-career families. The study would look at jobs, pay, housing, education and training, arts and culture, transportation, civic life, and barriers that make young people leave or stay away. The committee would then report its findings and recommendations to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR471.s: Would direct the Natural Resources Committee to study natural gas production issues in Nebraska. The study would look at whether companies have enough gas, pipelines, storage, and firm supply for home heating, power generation, ethanol production, and agriculture uses. It would also look at the cost of rising natural gas prices and then report its findings and recommendations.

NE-2025-LR472.s: The resolution would direct the Education Committee to study federally funded Head Start Preschool and Early Head Start programs in Nebraska. The study would look at their services, funding, staffing, background check rules, and how other states support them. The committee would then report its findings and policy recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR475.s: The resolution would order an interim study of state money given to nonprofit groups, especially groups that are tax-free under federal law. The study would look at who gets the money, where it comes from, how much is given, what it can be used for, and how well it is tracked. The Appropriations Committee would do the study and then report its findings and recommendations to lawmakers.

NE-2025-LR476.s: The Nebraska Legislature would direct the Nebraska Retirement Systems Committee to do an interim study on LB1095, a proposed law about moving retirement system assets out of investments tied to the People’s Republic of China. The study would look at fiscal, constitutional, and administrative issues, including costs, long-term revenue effects, and how the plan could be carried out. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or the Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR478.s: The resolution would assign the Health and Human Services Committee to study how Nebraska’s prescription drug monitoring program is run and operated, including how it works with the health information exchange. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or the Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR480.s: This resolution would direct the Education Committee to study how public money for youth development programs is spread across Nebraska. It would look for gaps in access, especially in rural areas and other low-resource communities, and review ways to better coordinate funding and improve results for youth, families, and communities. The committee would then report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or Legislative Council.

NE-2025-LR481.s: The resolution would direct the Health and Human Services Committee to study the fiscal and operational issues of adding long-term care services and supports to the state Medicaid managed care program. It would also look at what other states have spent and what problems they faced when making similar changes. After the study, the committee would report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature or the Legislative Council.
